newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's centre-right to back government on reform.
newsitem.headline: Italy's centre-right to back government on reform.

text.p: Centre-right Freedom Alliance leaders said on Monday they had decided to vote with the government on a plan to redraft Italy's constitution after a damaging split in the opposition put the whole process in doubt.

"The Freedom Alliance...will give an indication...in favour of the bi-cameral commission," Pierferdinando Casini, head of the centrist CCD party, told reporters after the bloc's leader Silvio Berlusconi met his partners to hammer out their stance.
"The Freedom Alliance is not divided," he added.
The upper house of parliament, the Senate, is due to vote on Thursday on a planned bi-cameral commission to work out changes to Italy's outdated 1948 constitution.

The vote, originally scheduled for Wednesday, ought to have been a formality -- the proposal was overwhelmingly endorsed by the Senate and Chamber of Deputies last summer and needs only a final green light from both houses to become law.
But the far-right National Alliance (AN) had been considering opposing the plan on its final reading.

AN leader Gianfranco Fini backed a proposal by ex-president Francesco Cossiga to deny the plan a two-thirds majority and thus force a referendum in favour of a constituent assembly to draft the reforms instead.

The split led to a battle of wills between Berlusconi and Fini, which politicians and commentators say amounted to a leadership struggle within the opposition bloc, but a face-saving compromise was finally achieved.
"I'm satisfied," Fini told reporters. "When you see the agenda we're preparing, you'll understand why."
AN has demanded guarantees on what reforms will be tackled, including a commitment to presidential-style government.
Giulio Maceratini, the party's leader in the Senate, told reporters after the meeting that the demands for guarantees would now be adopted as the bloc's official position.
Italy has been trying for 15 years to modernise its constitution to end a history of revolving door governments and instability.

It has twice set up bi-cameral commissions but progress has been negligible, despite the big corruption scandals of the early 1990s which felled the old ruling class and which many commentators believed would kick-start the reform process.

The Senate vote will be followed by a vote in the Chamber on January 21. If approved, the 70-member cross-party body will have until June 30 to draft reforms to the constitution. They would then go to parliament and subsequently to a referendum.

Massimo D'Alema, whose ex-communist Democratic Party of the Left is the biggest in Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government, has been the main sponsor of the bi-cameral commission and is considered a front runner to chair it.
He has said the government has an historic duty to achieve the reforms, which are expected to cover the powers and structure of parliament and government and federal devolution.
